questions.q: Why is recording `seed_simulator=42` alone not sufficient for reproducing a result, according to the lesson?
options: Seeds never actually affect simulator output
The same seed can produce different sampled outcomes on a different version of the simulator SDK, so the seed and the exact backend/SDK version must be recorded together
Seeds only matter for real hardware, not simulators
42 is an invalid seed value in Qiskit
questions.explain: If the simulator's internal pseudorandom algorithm changes between SDK versions, the same seed value can produce different outcomes -- meaning the seed is only meaningful when paired with the exact backend/SDK version from Lesson 15.

questions.q: What does `seed_transpiler` control, and why does the lesson say recording only `seed_simulator` but not `seed_transpiler` leaves a result only partially reproducible?
options: seed_transpiler controls shot count; omitting it only affects statistical noise slightly

seed_transpiler controls randomized qubit-layout/routing heuristics, which affect the actual circuit structure that runs -- omitting it means a re-run could execute a structurally different transpiled circuit even with the same simulator seed
seed_transpiler has no effect on anything and is safe to omit
seed_transpiler is identical to seed_simulator and recording one covers both
questions.explain: The transpiler seed affects which specific gate layout and qubit routing choices get made, which is a different (and separate) source of randomness from the simulator's measurement sampling -- both need to be recorded independently.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend recording a calibration timestamp instead of a seed for real-hardware experiments?
options: Real hardware runs always use seed_simulator=0 by convention

Physical hardware noise isn't seeded pseudorandomness -- it's a property of the device's current calibration state, which drifts over time, so a calibration timestamp explains result differences a seed never could
Calibration timestamps are required by IBM's terms of service
Hardware backends do not produce measurement counts
questions.explain: Unlike a simulator's pseudorandom generator, real hardware noise reflects the device's physical calibration state, which changes over time -- recording the calibration timestamp captures the relevant context for explaining variation between runs on the 'same' backend.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend generating the ExperimentRecord metadata programmatically rather than typing it by hand?
options: Programmatic generation is faster to type
Hand-typed records can silently drift from what actually ran, while a programmatically generated record reflects the real parameters used
Python dataclasses cannot be created manually
JSON files must always be auto-generated by law
questions.explain: A hand-typed metadata file risks a transcription error or going stale if the actual run used different parameters -- generating it programmatically from the same variables used to run the experiment avoids that drift.

questions.q: According to the lesson's worked example, what three things are jointly necessary (not independently sufficient) to make a reported experimental result reproducible?
options: A screenshot, a PDF report, and a spreadsheet
The git tag (code), the lockfile (environment), and the ExperimentRecord (seeds/shots/backend version)
Only the git tag is needed; the rest is optional
Only the shot count matters; code and environment are irrelevant
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties together Lesson 14 (git tag identifying code), Lesson 15 (lockfile identifying environment), and this lesson's ExperimentRecord (seeds, shots, backend version) as three jointly necessary pieces -- missing any one breaks reproducibility even if the other two are present.
